description: We’re a family team: Eldrich (11) does Arduino wiring, coding and testing, Hailey (10) leads sound design, story and the cardboard build, and Valentinus (parent) supervises safety and handles the submission. We built Earth Jukebox, a hardware + software project that turns NASA ocean temperature data into sound, vibration, light and a robot hand, so people who can’t see or can’t hear can explore it too. Our team is complete.
summary:
Earth Jukebox lets anyone hear and feel NASA ocean temperature data, including people who are blind, low-vision, Deaf or hard-of-hearing. Using frames from NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio (Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature), our web app turns each spot on the ocean into sound: warmer water plays higher notes, land goes quiet, and coastlines click. 

A cardboard controller built with an Arduino adds touch and sight. Two knobs move around the map, a vibration motor shakes harder over warm water, an LED blinks faster, and a 3D-printed robot hand raises more fingers as the water gets warmer. A button steps through the seasons so you can hear and feel the oceans change during the year. Most climate data is shared only as pictures. Earth Jukebox opens it up to people who can’t see it, and makes it more fun for everyone. It was built by two young makers, ages 11 and 10.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Earth Jukebox is a “jukebox” for ocean data. You move around a world map with two knobs, and the ocean temperature under the cursor comes out as sound, vibration, light and a robot hand. Every output follows one simple rule: higher = warmer. Higher note, stronger shake, faster blink, more fingers.

WHO IT HELPS

  • Blind and low-vision people: they explore by ear and by touch, without the screen. Notes rise with temperature, land goes quiet, coastlines click, and the “Where am I?” button reads out the place and temperature. A tactile cardboard map with the same layout as the data helps them find their way.
  • Deaf and hard-of-hearing people: they get the same information without sound. The vibration motor shakes harder, the LED blinks faster, and the robot hand raises 1 to 5 fingers as the water gets warmer (a fist means land). The screen also shows the place and temperature as text.
  • Everyone else: it makes climate data feel real and fun. You can hear the tropics “sing” and the poles go low, and hear Florida warm up between seasons.

HOW IT WORKS

  • Data: 12 monthly frames from NASA SVS #3912 (Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature, ECCO2 model by MIT/JPL).
  • Data to temperature: for each point, the web app reads the pixel colour and matches its hue to the visualization’s own colour bar (0 to 32 °C). Grey pixels are land.
  • Sound: tones are made live in the browser (Web Audio) on a pentatonic scale, so it always sounds musical.
  • Hardware: an Arduino Uno talks to the web page over USB (Web Serial). It reads 2 knobs and 4 buttons (pole-to-pole sweep, where am I, hand shows level, next season). It drives a vibration motor through an L298N driver, an LED, a buzzer, and a 3D-printed robot hand with 6 servos.
  • Checked against real values: Western Pacific warm pool about 30 °C, Indian Ocean about 29 °C, Southern Ocean about 2 °C, and Florida rising from 26 to 29 °C between seasons.

TOOLS
HTML, CSS, JavaScript (Web Audio, Web Serial, built-in text-to-speech), Arduino C++ with the Servo library, Arduino Uno, L298N motor driver, a motor from an old TT gear motor, servos, LED, buzzer, 3D printing and cardboard. Hosted on Cloudflare Pages.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE
We want any NASA image-based dataset to be explored without eyes or without ears. The same rule (higher = more) works for other data like rainfall, ice or air quality, so Earth Jukebox could become a library of “songs” about our planet for classrooms and accessibility centres.

BENEFITS

  • Opens NASA data that is usually shared only as pictures to people who can’t see it, and gives Deaf users a way to feel it without sound.
  • Anyone learns quickly: one rule (higher = warmer) works for every output, so you don’t need to read a legend.
  • Low cost: cardboard, an Arduino and a motor from an old toy. A school or library could build one.
  • Works in any modern Chrome or Edge browser, and the map and sounds still work without the hardware (mouse or keyboard only).

INTENDED IMPACT
We want any NASA image-based dataset to be explored without eyes or without ears. Our colour-to-value method works on other NASA visualizations with a colour bar, like rainfall, sea ice or air quality, so Earth Jukebox could become a library of “songs” about our planet for classrooms, museums and accessibility centres. It can also help people notice climate change: you can hear and feel warm water spreading between seasons.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

  • A “jukebox” for the Earth: you play the planet like an instrument.
  • The same data comes out four ways at once (sound, vibration, light and robot fingers), so people can use whichever sense works best for them.
  • A robot hand used as a data display: counting fingers is something everyone understands, even young kids.
  • Recycled parts: our vibration motor is the small motor from an old yellow toy gear motor, with a hot-glue blob on its shaft to make it shake.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

  • Accessibility first: everything works without looking at the screen. Every output has a backup in another sense, and the controls are big physical knobs and buttons.
  • Accuracy: we matched colours by hue, so dim streaks in the visualization still read correctly, and we checked our temperatures against known values.
  • Pleasant sound: a pentatonic scale means it never sounds harsh, even when moving fast.
  • Safety: the motor stops by itself if the computer disconnects, the robot hand’s servos move one at a time so USB power isn’t overloaded, and the motor runs from its own battery through a driver board.
  • Simplicity: built by two young makers (11 and 10) with beginner tools, so others can copy it.

TEAM
Eldrich (11): Arduino wiring, coding and testing. Hailey (10): sound design, story and the cardboard build. Valentinus (parent): supervision and safety, helped write this project page, and handled the accounts and submission.

AI USE
The web app code was written with Claude3, following our team’s idea and sound design. The Arduino code, the idea, the sound design, the hardware build and all testing are our team’s own work. The spoken descriptions use the browser’s built-in text-to-speech voice.
